claims.text: The starting material is a CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy forming a solid solution.
Valence electron concentration controls superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Valence electron concentration influences the density of states at the Fermi level.
Higher valence electron concentration can lead to a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Elemental substitution can vary valence electron concentration while preserving the high-entropy-alloy definition.
Changing valence electron concentration through substitution changes local lattice distortion.
Changing valence electron concentration through substitution changes atomic-scale disorder.
A high-entropy alloy with a valence electron concentration near 4.5–5.5 will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
The proposed comparison is to be performed at cryogenic temperatures.
The proposed comparison covers magnetic fields up to 5 T.
The control is CoCrFeMnNi without intentional variation of its valence electron concentration.
Lattice distortion may independently affect superconducting behavior.
Magnetic interactions may independently affect superconducting behavior.
A lack of a significant association between valence electron concentration and superconducting behavior would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that higher VEC may increase Tc, whereas the prediction favors a VEC of 4.5–5.5. CoCrFeMnNi has a nominal average VEC near 8 under conventional electron counting, so moving the stated baseline toward 4.5–5.5 would lower rather than raise VEC. The claimed direction is therefore internally inconsistent.
